description: We are a team focused on developing a video game with social and aerospace impact, designed to raise awareness through an immersive, entertaining, and high-value experience. We currently have solid experience in technology project development, programming, and structuring. We are enthusiastic about space exploration, science communication, and creating interactive experiences with a purpose.
summary: This project focuses on the development of an educational video game using augmented reality and educational content from NASA resources, as provided in the NASA Space Challenge competition, with the goal of simplifying the space engineering dilemmas that define a real space mission in order to better capture the attention of young people in a more educational, immersive, and entertaining way. Given the challenges of effectively capturing young people’s attention and the overreliance on AI tools—which has increased the demand for games that can support both learning and entertainment— an immersive approach is proposed that applies augmented reality to a 2D game featuring eight AI-generated scenarios. These scenarios tell a gripping story about a group of high school students from Cajamarca who must save a lunar colony from invasion by the Queen of the Void, during which they will learn about real lunar space missions through immersive simulations. The developed system aims to support educational processes and enhance interdisciplinary development using official NASA content, contributing to immersive space education in communities via online platforms. The results show that the use of augmented reality improves educational contextual coherence, enhances students’ talents, and reduces attention lapses among young people, positioning the technology as a strategic tool for inclusive, immersive education on space missions.
details:
Greg and the Last Colony

Explore. Learn. Play. Save the Moon!

Github repository: https://github.com/MrPC7/greg-last-colony-game/tree/main

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Greg and the Last Colony is a free, bilingual (English and Spanish), browser-based educational adventure game that transforms lunar exploration and Earth science into interactive challenges.

Set in the year 2087, the story follows Greg, a student from Cajamarca, Peru, who dreams of becoming an astronaut. Alongside his friends Elen and Joseph, and guided by Orbi, an alien archivist, he discovers a mysterious signal called NOX-Ω coming from the Moon.

Players explore their school, complete interactive STEM activities, recover five energy cores, and eventually travel to the Moon to save Selene, the Last Colony, from the Queen of the Void.

The game features hands-on mini-games covering lunar physics, gravity, astronaut training, radiation protection, thermal control, solar energy, and the history of lunar missions. It also incorporates real NASA datasets through Ray's Signal, where players explore global temperature trends using NASA GISTEMP and active fire observations using NASA FIRMS.

Players navigate the school environment, interact with different learning zones, collect rewards, unlock achievements, and complete a final mission challenge. The game also includes an augmented reality camera experience, bilingual content, mobile-friendly controls, and a downloadable mission completion certificate.

2. What benefits does it have?

The project makes complex scientific concepts more accessible, engaging, and enjoyable through experiential learning.

Its main benefits include:

  • STEM education: Introduces physics, astronomy, mathematics, engineering, and environmental science through practical challenges.
  • Scientific literacy: Encourages students to interpret real NASA data rather than simply reading scientific information.
  • Gamified learning: Uses achievements, stars, collectibles, missions, and rewards to encourage participation.
  • Accessibility: Runs on modern web browsers without requiring installation or user registration.
  • Bilingual education: Supports English and Spanish, making the experience accessible to a wider student community.
  • Digital skills: Encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, experimentation, and technology awareness.
  • Environmental awareness: Connects lunar exploration with real challenges on Earth, including global temperature changes and wildfires.

Students can earn a downloadable Selene Explorer certificate after completing the missions and defeating the Queen of the Void.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our main objective is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, innovators, and space explorers, particularly students from communities with limited access to advanced STEM learning experiences.

We chose Cajamarca, Peru, as the starting point of the story to demonstrate that curiosity, scientific talent, and innovation can emerge anywhere.

By connecting a local school environment with lunar exploration and real NASA datasets, we aim to:

  • Promote inclusive access to science and technology education.
  • Encourage more young people to pursue STEM careers.
  • Strengthen scientific and environmental awareness.
  • Make space exploration understandable through interactive experiences.
  • Demonstrate how open scientific data can be transformed into meaningful educational tools.
  • Inspire students to see themselves as future contributors to science and space exploration.

Ultimately, we want students to understand that space exploration is not just about reaching the Moon: It's about developing the knowledge and skills to solve real-world problems.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

The current MVP was developed as a web application using modern frontend technologies and open scientific datasets.

Software and technologies:

  • Next.js 16 – application framework and routing.
  • React 19 – interactive user interfaces.
  • TypeScript – application logic and type safety.
  • Zustand – game state management and local progress saving.
  • Tailwind CSS 4 and CSS Modules – responsive interface design.
  • Chart.js and react-chartjs-2 – scientific data visualization.
  • HTML Canvas and getUserMedia – camera-based augmented reality experience.
  • SVG – interactive visual elements and fire map.
  • Web Audio API – dynamically generated sound effects and music.
  • Python 3 – NASA dataset processing and preparation.
  • Pillow – image watermarking.
  • GitHub and GitHub Actions – version control, collaboration, and automated deployment.

Scientific resources:

  • NASA GISTEMP v4 – global land-ocean temperature anomalies.
  • NASA FIRMS – satellite-based active fire observations.
  • NASA lunar science resources.
  • NASA Apollo and Artemis mission documentation.
  • NASA spacesuit and space radiation educational resources.

Hardware: The game is designed to work on standard computers, laptops, and smartphones. Its camera-based AR functionality uses compatible mobile devices. No specialized physical hardware is required.

Future development: The complete expanded version is planned for Unity with C# and AR Foundation, enabling more immersive 3D environments, interactive lunar exploration, and advanced augmented reality experiences.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

Our creativity comes from combining an original science-fiction narrative with real scientific knowledge and interactive learning.

Instead of presenting science as a traditional lesson, we turn each concept into a challenge that players must solve to advance the story.

Some examples include:

  • Landing a spacecraft while considering lunar gravity and descent speed.
  • Building a radiation shield while managing limited material mass.
  • Exploring why astronauts can jump approximately six times higher on the Moon.
  • Managing oxygen production and temperature inside a lunar greenhouse.
  • Exploring the chronological history of lunar missions.
  • Using augmented reality to visualize the Moon, lunar landers, spacesuits, and radiation concepts.
  • Analyzing real NASA temperature and wildfire datasets through interactive activities.

Another distinctive feature is the connection between Cajamarca and the Moon. The adventure begins in a familiar school environment and gradually transforms into an ambitious interplanetary mission.

We also designed Orbi as an interactive guide who introduces scientific facts and helps players understand concepts through storytelling.

The combination of storytelling, gamification, bilingual learning, open NASA data, and accessible web technology makes the experience both educational and entertaining.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several important factors throughout the development process:

Scientific accuracy: Educational challenges are grounded in NASA resources and established scientific principles. Fictional elements, such as the Queen of the Void and her gravitational powers, are distinguished from real science.

Accessibility and inclusion: We designed a free browser-based experience that works on computers and smartphones, supports Spanish and English, and does not require an account or installation.

Educational engagement: Activities are designed to encourage experimentation, active participation, and problem-solving rather than passive information consumption.

Environmental relevance: We integrated real NASA Earth observation data to connect space exploration with environmental challenges on our own planet.

Technical feasibility: We prioritized a functional web-based MVP that could be developed, tested, and accessed without specialized equipment or expensive infrastructure.

User experience: We considered intuitive navigation, mobile-friendly controls, visual storytelling, interactive rewards, and clear educational feedback.

Responsible use of technology: We documented our scientific sources and the use of AI-generated visual assets and AI-assisted programming. The project does not claim NASA endorsement or affiliation.

Our vision

Greg and the Last Colony is more than a space adventure. It is an invitation for young people to explore science, develop their creativity, and discover their potential.

We believe that every student should have the opportunity to imagine themselves as a scientist, engineer, or astronaut, regardless of where they come from.

From Cajamarca to the Moon, every discovery brings us closer to a better future.
